claims.text: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies and limited room-temperature tensile ductility with brittle behavior.
A short-duration anneal below the recrystallization threshold will form nanoscale twins along lamellar colony boundaries.
The structural mediator produced by the treatment is nanotwins localized at lamellar colony boundaries.
Boundary nanotwins act as nanoscale barriers to dislocation motion.
The nanotwins provide an alternative dislocation-motion pathway that produces lower stress concentrations.
Interrupting dislocation pile-ups reduces excessive local stress accumulation at internal boundaries.
Reducing local stress accumulation suppresses microcracking and catastrophic damage during straining.
The induced nanotwins contribute to strength through twin strengthening.
The annealed alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will retain or increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The predicted improvements apply under room-temperature tensile loading.
The amount of nanotwin formation and the magnitude of property changes depend on annealing temperature and duration.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires increased ductility together with retained or enhanced strength, but the falsification rule parenthetically joins lack of ductility improvement and lack of strength retention with 'and.' Thus, failure to improve ductility may not falsify the hypothesis if strength is merely retained, despite contradicting the stated prediction.
